checks.claim: Lind took twelve scurvy patients aboard the Salisbury, 20 May 1747
checks.note: Lind's text: 'On the 20th of May 1747, I took twelve patients in the scurvy, on board the Salisbury at sea.' Grokipedia James_Lind and Wikipedia agree.

checks.claim: All twelve shared one sick berth and one diet
checks.note: Lind: they lay together in one place, a proper apartment for the sick in the fore-hold, with one diet common to all. Grokipedia: housed together on a standard diet.

checks.claim: Remedies included cider, vinegar, seawater, and two oranges and one lemon a day; one remedy per pair
checks.note: Six pairs: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water (half a pint a day), two oranges and one lemon, an electuary of garlic, mustard seed etc.

checks.claim: In six days one of the fruit pair was fit for duty; no other pair mended so fast
checks.note: Lind: 'one of those who had taken them, being at the end of 6 days fit for duty'; the most sudden and visible good effects were from the oranges and lemons; cider next best but slower.

checks.claim: Key: the other five pairs, on the same berth and diet, rule out rest and the ship's food as the cure
checks.note: Sound inference, but it leans on the pairs being alike at the start (Lind gave the seawater to the two worst cases, so they were not all alike). That is the judge's clarity point, not a factual error.

checks.claim: Wrong: luck ruled out
checks.note: Two men a pair; Grokipedia notes the trial's small scale. Luck is not ruled out.

checks.claim: Wrong: mildest cases ruled out
checks.note: Lind chose the allocation himself and picked cases 'as similar as I could have them'; that does not rule out the fruit pair being milder. Correctly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: any fresh fruit would have healed as fast
checks.note: No other fruit was tried.

checks.claim: Quote: 'as similar as I could have them'
checks.note: Sutton 2003 (JRSM) and sportsci.org both quote Lind: 'Their cases were as similar as I could have them.'

checks.claim: Quote: oranges and lemons were 'the most effectual remedies for this distemper at sea'
checks.note: Lind 1753: 'the result of all my experiments was, that oranges and lemons were the most effectual remedies for this distemper at sea.'

checks.claim: Lind decided for himself which patient got each remedy
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'non-random assignment'. Lind's own text puts the two worst patients on seawater. The JLL notes Lind never states his allocation method, but his choosing at least the seawater pair is in his own words, so the stem holds.

checks.claim: Quote: seawater went to 'the worst patients'
checks.note: Lind: 'Two of the worst patients, with the tendons in the ham rigid, (a symptom none of the rest had), were put under a course of sea-water.'

checks.claim: The seawater pair were 'the only two whose hand tendons had gone stiff'
checks.note: Lind wrote 'with the tendons in the ham rigid' (the ham is the back of the knee, the hamstring tendons; rigid hams are a classic scurvy sign Lind describes elsewhere). Every transcription checked (sportsci.org, Helsinki scans of the 1753 text, the Nutrition Reviews reprint) reads 'ham'; 'hand' is a transcription slip in the American Revolution Institute excerpt, and one OCR reads 'L arm'. The part about 'a symptom none of the rest had' is right. Fix: 'the only two whose tendons behind the knee had gone stiff', or drop the detail and keep 'the worst patients'.

checks.claim: Key: letting chance assign stops the doctor choosing
checks.note: Random allocation removes selection by the investigator and balances known and unknown factors.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: matching by hand, blinding the patient, a dummy treatment do not take the choosing away
checks.note: Blinding and placebo address other biases; matching leaves the doctor choosing.

checks.claim: Context: random numbers in sealed envelopes in Austin Bradford Hill's 1948 streptomycin trial
checks.note: MRC 1948: allocation by 'a statistical series based on random sampling numbers drawn up ... by Professor Bradford Hill', unknown to the investigators and 'contained in a set of sealed envelopes'. Grokipedia RCT: 'led by statistician Austin Bradford Hill', 'random allocation via sealed envelopes'. Strictly, Hill was one of three designers (with D'Arcy Hart and Daniels); 'Hill's trial' is the usual shorthand.

checks.claim: Context: chance evens out, on average, differences no one thought of
checks.note: Grokipedia: randomisation 'balances both known and unknown confounders'.

checks.claim: A Treatise of the Scurvy published 1753
checks.note: Grokipedia, Wikipedia and the JLL record (Lind J 1753, Edinburgh) all give 1753.

checks.claim: The trial filled only a few paragraphs of a long book
checks.note: Wikipedia: the experiment 'occupied only a few paragraphs in a work that was long and complex and had little impact'.

checks.claim: The Royal Navy issued lemon juice to every warship only in 1795
checks.note: June 1795: the Admiralty agreed that lemon juice and sugar be issued daily to the crews of all warships. Grokipedia: 1795, a daily ration of three-quarters of an ounce (after six weeks at sea).

checks.claim: Key: Lind held that scurvy has several causes, damp air among them
checks.note: Wikipedia: Lind 'shared medical opinion at the time that scurvy had multiple causes', among them salt meat eaten in a damp atmosphere. PMC4337985: he thought it came from perspiration thwarted by moisture in the air plus a salt-meat diet. Wikipedia (Lind): multiple causes needing multiple remedies.

checks.claim: Wrong: lack of one thing in the diet
checks.note: Bartholomew 2002: 'Lind conceived of scurvy not as a disease of dietary deficiency, but of faulty digestion.'

checks.claim: Wrong: boiled lemon juice loses its power
checks.note: Lind promoted the boiled 'rob' to carry to sea, not knowing the boiling destroyed the vitamin C; no source found where he held the opposite.

checks.claim: Wrong: cured by fresh fruit and nothing else
checks.note: JLL: 'Lind nowhere states clearly that citrus juice is a cure for scurvy'; he still named malt as a cure in the third edition. Wikipedia: he 'never actively promoted lemon juice as a single cure'.

checks.claim: Context: salt meat eaten in damp air that held back sweating; a fault of digestion rather than a lack in the diet
checks.note: JLL: 'a disease of faulty digestion and excretion, exacerbated by environment'; Wikipedia: a damp atmosphere preventing healthful perspiration.

checks.claim: Context: the rob; boiling destroyed the vitamin C
checks.note: JLL: the rob 'has subsequently been shown to contain practically no vitamin C'. Wikipedia: boiling 'destroyed the vitamin C'. 'Rob' is Lind's own word ('the rob or extract').

checks.claim: Context: the Navy acted after a scurvy-free voyage on lemon juice and the urging of Gilbert Blane
checks.note: Wikipedia: after HMS Suffolk's scurvy-free voyage (reached India March 1795) and the writings of Blane and Thomas Trotter; JLL quotes Harvie: 'Only in 1795, when ... Gilbert Blane championed Lind's work, were the Sea Lords persuaded to act.' Grokipedia: championed by Blane and Trotter.

checks.claim: Angina: chest pain when the heart gets too little blood
Surgeons tied off two arteries in the chest wall (internal mammary ligation); early reports said most patients improved
checks.note: Fieschi (1939) tied both internal mammary arteries; reported that three-quarters of his patients improved and up to a third seemed cured; the operation became popular.

checks.claim: Leonard Cobb's team in Seattle, 1959, 17 patients: 8 ligated, 9 skin incisions only
checks.note: Cobb LA, Thomas GI, Dillard DH, Merendino KA, Bruce RA, NEJM 1959;260:1115-1118 (University of Washington, Seattle). SBM: 17 patients, eight with both arteries tied, nine with skin incisions in the same place. Grokipedia Sham_surgery: 17 patients, skin incisions mimicking the exposure.

checks.claim: Patients were not told which they had
checks.note: Double-blind: neither the patients nor the physicians assessing them knew the assignment.

checks.claim: About as many improved in each group
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'comparable symptom relief, with roughly 63% of patients in each reporting improvement'; SBM: 'the results were the same'.

checks.claim: Key: the tying added nothing; wrong choices (both mended the heart; pain imagined; any small operation cures)
checks.note: Sham comparison showed no advantage of ligation; nothing showed either operation mended the heart.

checks.claim: Context: the operation was soon given up
checks.note: Grokipedia: the sham trials (1959-1960) led to its abandonment; SBM: 'the beginning of the end'.

checks.claim: Henry Beecher, a Harvard anaesthetist
checks.note: Anaesthetist-in-Chief at MGH; Henry Isaiah Dorr Professor of Anaesthesia Research at Harvard (1941).

checks.claim: 'The Powerful Placebo' (1955): fifteen trials, 1,082 patients
checks.note: Grokipedia: 15 double-blind trials, 1,082 patients.

checks.claim: About a third relieved by a dummy pill alone
checks.note: Beecher's own figure 35.2% +/- 2.2% 'satisfactorily relieved by a placebo'; Kienle and Kiene's abstract: about a third. Grokipedia rounds to about 30%; 'about a third' matches Beecher's paper.

checks.claim: Kienle and Kiene, 1997, found no evidence of a placebo effect in any of the trials
checks.note: J Clin Epidemiol 1997;50:1311-1318: 'no evidence was found of any placebo effect in any of the studies cited by him.' (They could assess 14 of the 15 for detail, per The New Atlantis; the abstract's claim covers all.)

checks.claim: Key: a no-pill group followed the same way shows the dummy's own effect; Beecher's trials had none
checks.note: Grokipedia attributes Beecher's figure to 'the absence of no-treatment control groups for comparison'; Liberman (1962, quoted in The New Atlantis) found no placebo experiments with untreated controls. Grokipedia's Placebo page says 'most trials' of the era; no source found showing any Beecher trial had a no-treatment arm.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: real drug, open-label dummy, healthy people
checks.note: None isolates the dummy's own effect from natural recovery and regression to the mean; Wikipedia: those are ruled out by comparing placebo with no treatment.

checks.claim: Context: natural recovery, fluctuation, regression to the mean inflate a placebo arm
checks.note: Kienle and Kiene list spontaneous improvement, fluctuation of symptoms and regression to the mean among the causes of false placebo impressions.

checks.claim: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche, 2001 (NEJM), 114 trials comparing placebo with no treatment
checks.note: NEJM 2001;344:1594-1602. 130 trials met the criteria; 114 had usable data (32 binary, 82 continuous). Grokipedia Placebo: 114 analysed, 8,525 patients.

checks.claim: About 40 different illnesses
checks.note: Full text: 'The trials investigated 40 clinical conditions.'

checks.claim: Key: small effects on what patients felt, such as pain
checks.note: Possible small benefits on continuous subjective outcomes; in 27 pain trials a 6.5 mm drop on a 100 mm scale.

checks.claim: Wrong: small effects on test results such as blood pressure
checks.note: No significant effect on objective outcomes (pooled SMD -0.12, CI -0.27 to 0.03).

checks.claim: Wrong: large effects; no effects at all, not even on pain
checks.note: 'little evidence ... that placebos had powerful clinical effects'; pain did show a small significant effect.

checks.claim: Context: against no treatment, placebos did nothing measurable to the illnesses; patients reported a little less pain
checks.note: 'no significant effects on objective or binary outcomes'. Accurate as the review's finding; the 2010 Cochrane update (202 trials) agreed. Attributing it to the review (the judge's stance point) is wise but not a factual fix.

checks.claim: Steven Cummings's team; women on an osteoporosis medicine; hip scans each year
checks.note: Cummings SR et al. (Fracture Intervention Trial), JAMA 2000;283:1318-1321; alendronate; hip and spine BMD at baseline, 12 and 24 months (abstract read via Europe PMC).

checks.claim: Of women whose hip bone fell by more than 4% in year one, 83% gained in year two on the same medicine
checks.note: '83% (95% CI, 82%-84%) had increases in hip BMD during the second year', mean gain 4.7%.

checks.claim: Women who gained 8% or more in year one lost a little on average in year two
checks.note: 'lost an average of 1% (95% CI, 0.1%-1.9%) during the next year'. Similar results with raloxifene.

checks.claim: Key: regression to the mean; wrong choices (a year's delay, bone rests, scanners reset)
checks.note: The paper's own title names regression to the mean; the delay and rest choices explain one direction only; nothing indicates a scanner change.

checks.claim: Context: the doctor who tries a new medicine on her sickest patients sees many improve
checks.note: Morton and Torgerson (BMJ 2003): treating clinical outliers 'will usually produce a gratifying and sharp response to treatment because of regression to the mean'.

checks.claim: John Noseworthy's team, 1994, Canadian trial of MS treatments
checks.note: Noseworthy JH et al., Neurology 1994;44:16-20, 'the physician-blinded Canadian cooperative trial' (abstract read via Europe PMC).

checks.claim: MS a disease of the brain and spinal cord; plasma exchange swaps out the liquid part of the blood
checks.note: Grokipedia: MS a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system; plasmapheresis removes and replaces plasma.

checks.claim: Each patient examined by two neurologists at every check-up, one blinded and one not
checks.note: 'All patients were examined by both a blinded and an unblinded neurologist at each assessment in this trial.'

checks.claim: Only the unblinded neurologists scored the plasma-exchange group as doing better than the sham group
checks.note: Unblinded scores showed an apparent benefit for group II (plasma exchange plus oral cyclophosphamide and prednisone) at 6, 12 and 24 months; blinded scores did not. Group III had sham exchange and placebo drugs.

checks.claim: Key and wrong choices
checks.note: Conclusion: 'Physician blinding prevented an erroneous conclusion about treatment efficacy (false positive, type 1 error)'; so not a missed benefit; the same patients were scored by both, so not patient belief; no sign the sham harmed.

checks.claim: Context: judged blind, neither treatment beat the sham; the authors wrote that blinding saved them from a false conclusion
checks.note: Fair paraphrase of the conclusion quoted above.

checks.claim: Placebo areas: about 200,000 vaccinated and about 200,000 given the dummy
checks.note: Francis 1955: 200,745 vaccinated, 201,229 placebo.

checks.claim: Paralytic polio: 33 vaccinated, 115 placebo
Key: 2,000 a group gives too few cases to tell apart
checks.note: At 16 and 57 per 100,000, 2,000 a group expects about 0.3 and 1.1 cases, about 1.5 in all; Meier shows even 40,000 a group gives a gap chance could explain.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: no gap proves failure; same gap cheaper; clear gap if randomised
checks.note: Randomising does not supply the missing cases.

checks.claim: Context: a hundredth of the children; one or two cases in all; rare disease; about 1.8 million enrolled; Thomas Francis's trial
checks.note: Grokipedia: about 1.8 million children, directed by Thomas Francis Jr.; Francis's tables total 1,829,916. Meldrum (BMJ 1998): 'a disease of relatively low incidence'.

checks.claim: Placebo areas: volunteers got vaccine or dummy; refusers got nothing
checks.note: Francis: children whose parents requested participation, half to vaccine and half to placebo; 338,778 not inoculated. (Meier's Table 1 notes the not-inoculated group includes 8,577 children who got one or two placebo shots; close enough for 'got nothing' at this grade.)

checks.claim: Paralytic rates per 100,000: dummy 57, refused 36
checks.note: Table 3: placebo 115 cases (57); not inoculated 121 cases (36).

checks.claim: Neither group had the vaccine
checks.note: The vaccine was licensed only on 12 April 1955, the day the results were announced.

checks.claim: Key: families who sign up differ
checks.note: Francis: 'the nonrequesting population might well be a more resistant group than the inoculated'; Meier: the volunteer effect is 'clearly evident'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the dummy shot raised the risk; chance; vaccinated elsewhere
checks.note: Observed-area refusers, with no shots given to anyone in their comparison, also ran lower (35 against 46), and the volunteers-to-refusers ratio is about the same in both designs, so the shot is not the cause; 115 against 121 cases on these group sizes is far beyond chance; no vaccine existed outside the trial. The judge's point stands that the stem alone does not rule out the shot.

checks.claim: Context: volunteers better off; polio hit hardest the hygienically better off; observed-area refusers lower too
checks.note: Meier: volunteers 'more well-to-do'; polio 'seemed to hit hardest those who were better off hygienically'. Francis: 'the uninoculated - or refused - portion of the second grade in observed areas also had a lower rate' (35 against 46).

checks.claim: Context: '16 cases in 100,000 among the vaccinated against 57 led Thomas Francis to report the vaccine 80 to 90 percent effective against paralytic polio'
checks.note: 16 against 57 is a cut of about 72 percent (Francis's Table 7: 72% for all paralytic cases in the placebo areas). Francis's 80 to 90 percent was for 'laboratory confirmed cases of paralytic poliomyelitis' ('taking the composite results against laboratory confirmed cases ... an effectiveness of 80 to 90% was observed in the placebo study areas'). A student who works 1 - 16/57 gets 72 and sees the clash. Fix: 'There the vaccinated fell ill at 16 in 100,000 against 57, a cut of about 72 percent; counting only the cases the laboratory confirmed as polio, Thomas Francis put the vaccine at 80 to 90 percent effective against paralytic polio.' Or drop the percentage.

unit_notes: Checked 2026-11-27 against Grokipedia, Wikipedia, the JLL, Lind's 1753 text (sportsci.org transcription; Helsinki scans via search), Francis 1955 (UNL transcription), Meier, and the PubMed abstracts via Europe PMC. Two errors: Lind's seawater pair had 'the tendons in the ham rigid' (back of the knee), not the hand (04c19ebef4; facts.md F3 carries the same slip from the American Revolution Institute excerpt); and 251ff949de's context ties Francis's 80-90 percent to the 16-vs-57 rates, which give about 72 percent; the 80-90 figure is for laboratory-confirmed paralytic cases. facts.md F24 should note that the 80-90 percent is for lab-confirmed cases. Beecher's percentage: his paper says 35.2 percent, Grokipedia rounds to about 30; 'about a third' is right. Cobb's 17 patients (8 against 9) come from Science-Based Medicine and Grokipedia; the NEJM full text was not reachable, but both agree. Nothing in the unit changes over time.
